column1: # The PRODUCTION-SHAPED cluster's topics.
# One row per topic, tab-separated, in this order:
#   name <TAB> partitions <TAB> replication <TAB> configs
# "configs" is a SEMICOLON-separated list of Kafka topic-level configuration keys, passed straight
# through to `kafka-topics.sh --config`. Use `-` for "no configuration, take the broker defaults".
# Semicolons rather than commas because a Kafka config VALUE can itself contain a comma:
# `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` is one setting, not two. Every key here is a real Kafka topic
# config; a typo makes topic creation fail loudly rather than quietly producing a topic that
# behaves differently from what this file claims.
# Retention is written in milliseconds because that is the unit `retention.ms` takes. The comment
# beside each row says what it is in human units.
# WHAT THIS CLUSTER IS FOR
# This is the one that has to look like a system somebody is actually running. Sixteen topics with
# names that read like a business rather than like a test fixture, partition counts from 1 to 24
# because real clusters are never uniform, and a replication factor of three throughout — which is
# the point of running three brokers, because in-sync replicas, leaders and preferred-leader
# imbalance are things a single-broker cluster simply cannot show.
# REPLICATION AND min.insync.replicas. `replication` is how many copies of each partition exist;
# `min.insync.replicas` is how many of them must acknowledge a write before the producer is told
# it succeeded. Almost every topic here is 3 and 2: three copies, and writes keep working when one
# broker is down. `shipping.dispatches` is the deliberate exception at 3 and 3, so that losing a
# single broker makes that one topic — and only that one — start rejecting writes with
# NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS while the rest of the cluster carries on. That is the failure the demo wants
# to show, and it is the honest way to show it: an under-replicated partition is a fact about a
# cluster with a missing broker, not something a seed script can write in from outside.
# `clickstream.raw` and `platform.metrics` are at replication 2, not 3, because that is what
# people really do with high-volume data they can afford to lose — and because a topic list where
# every row says "3" teaches you nothing about the column.
# The busiest keyed stream: the shape most systems' most important topic has. Twelve partitions
# because it has been scaled up at least once, which is why the number is not a power of anything
# meaningful.
orders.v1
# 7 days.
# Money moves less and is kept longer.
payments.transactions
# 30 days.
# THE DELIBERATELY FRAGILE ONE. min.insync.replicas equals the replication factor, so all three
# copies must acknowledge every write. Stop any one broker and this topic goes read-only while
# everything else keeps working. See the section above.
shipping.dispatches
# 14 days.
# Invoices: few partitions, very long retention, and a hard message-size ceiling because an
# invoice with two thousand line items is a bug rather than a large invoice.
billing.invoices
# 180 days.
# Outbound notifications: email, push, SMS. Short retention — a notification nobody sent within
# the hour is not worth sending — and the delete policy stated explicitly rather than inherited.
notifications.outbound
# 6 hours.
# Fraud scores, one per order. Small, keyed, and read by a service that must never fall behind.
fraud.scores
# 3 days.
# The firehose: twenty-four partitions, no keys, one day of retention or a gigabyte per partition,
# whichever runs out first. This is the topic that makes the message browser's virtualised table
# and its offset seek do real work, and the one whose partition list does not fit on a screen.
analytics.pageviews
# 1 day, or 1 GiB per partition.
# Raw clickstream, keyed by session so one visitor's clicks stay on one partition and a
# partition-filtered browse returns a coherent story rather than a shuffled one. Replication 2:
# this is the data you can afford to lose some of.
clickstream.raw
# 12 hours.
# Per-minute service metrics. Replication 2 for the same reason as above.
platform.metrics
# 2 days.
# A compacted topic is a keyed table, not a log: Kafka keeps the newest value for each key for ever
# and throws older ones away. KUI draws these differently, which is why there are three.
# The customer table.
customers.profiles
# The search index, at volume: thousands of records over a few hundred keys, six per cent of them
# tombstones. This is where you go to see what compaction and deletion look like on a topic too
# big to read by eye.
search.index-updates
# compact AND delete together: keep the latest value per key, but also drop anything older than
# the retention window. Stock levels for a product nobody sells any more should eventually go.
inventory.stock-levels
# 14 days.
# Plain-text log lines. The message browser has to show a value it cannot parse as JSON without
# pretending it failed, so every cluster in this demo has one.
audit.log.raw
# 90 days.
# The dead-letter queue for orders.v1: where a message goes when a consumer cannot process it.
# Small, and interesting precisely because it is not empty. Its headers name real partitions and
# offsets in orders.v1, so opening one dead letter tells you where to look next.
orders.v1.DLQ
# 14 days.
# A topic created for a service that has not shipped yet. No data file, so it is created and left
# EMPTY. An empty topic is a real state and a topic list where every row has records never shows
# you what zero looks like.
loyalty.points
# 30 days.
# A leading underscore is the convention for "this belongs to a piece of infrastructure, not to
# you", and user interfaces hide these behind a "show internal topics" switch.
_schemas
